Kainji Hydroelectric and Solar Hybrid Plant – Engineering Specification

Document No: KHP-ENG-SPEC-014 Rev. 4.2
Effective Date: 2026-03-18
Issuing Authority: Plant Engineering Department, Kainji HEP
Status: Current Controlled Document
Supersedes: Rev. 4.1 (dated 2024-11-30, now archived)

1. GENERAL PLANT CAPABILITY

The Kainji Hydroelectric and Solar Hybrid Plant has_capacity_mw is 760 MW. Record status: current. This figure represents the net dependable capacity at the generator terminals under the current operating configuration, including the integrated solar field output during daylight hours. This value is the basis for all system planning, load dispatch agreements, and transmission interface studies. No derating is applied for ambient temperature or reservoir elevation within the normal operating band.

The plant comprises twelve main generating units, a 60 MWp solar PV array on the east embankment, and a 40 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) for grid stabilisation. The solar and BESS components are synchronised through the existing 330 kV switchyard.

2. HYDRAULIC AND CIVIL WORKS

2.1 Dam Structure and Reservoir
The main dam is a zoned earth-fill embankment with a crest length of 8,040 m and a maximum height of 64 m above the lowest foundation level. Structural design safety factor for static loading: 2.0. Dynamic (seismic) safety factor: 1.5, based on a design ground acceleration of 0.08g. The spillway comprises six radial gates, each 12.5 m wide, with a combined discharge capacity of 20,000 m³/s at maximum flood level.

Reservoir top water level (normal): 141.5 m above datum.
Minimum operating level for power generation: 132.0 m above datum.
Usable storage: 11.5 km³.

2.2 Intake and Penstock
Each of the twelve intakes is fitted with a coarse trash rack (bar spacing 120 mm) and a fixed-wheel gate. The penstocks are steel-lined concrete conduits, diameter 6.8 m, with a design head of 38 m at rated flow. Hydraulic design margin on penstock pressure: 15% above maximum static head.

2.3 Tailrace
The tailrace channel is designed for a maximum discharge of 2,800 m³/s without exceeding a tailwater elevation of 118.0 m.

3. ELECTROMECHANICAL EQUIPMENT

3.1 Turbines
Twelve vertical-shaft Francis turbines, each rated at 68 MW at a net head of 36.5 m. Turbine design speed: 100 rpm. Runner diameter: 4.2 m. Each turbine is fitted with a digital electro-hydraulic governor, speed regulation range ± 0.5% under isolated operation.

3.2 Generators
Each turbine is coupled to a 75 MVA synchronous generator, 12 kV, 50 Hz, 0.9 power factor lagging. Generator cooling is closed-circuit air-water, with a design cooling water flow of 1,200 m³/h per unit. Stator winding insulation class F, temperature rise limit 105 K. Excitation is via static thyristor systems with automatic voltage regulation.

3.3 Transformers
Twelve generator step-up transformers, each rated 80 MVA, 12/330 kV, ONAN/ONAF cooling. Impedance: 12.5% at rated MVA. The transformers are located in a dedicated bay adjacent to the powerhouse. Design ambient temperature for loading calculations: 40°C, with a maximum winding hot-spot temperature of 120°C under continuous rated load.

3.4 Switchyard (330 kV)
The 330 kV switchyard is a double-bus, single-breaker arrangement with a total of 14 bays. Circuit breakers are SF6 type, rated 63 kA symmetrical interrupting capacity. Current transformers: 1,200:5 A, class 5P30. The switchyard is designed for a maximum continuous current of 3,150 A per busbar. Busbar design margins are per IEC 62271-1, with a short-time withstand current of 63 kA for 3 seconds.

4. SOLAR PV AND BESS AUXILIARY SYSTEMS

4.1 Solar PV Array
The 60 MWp PV array comprises 132,000 bifacial monocrystalline modules, each rated 455 Wp. The array is divided into 24 inverters stations, each with a 2.5 MVA central inverter. The DC/AC ratio is 1.15. The array is mounted on single-axis trackers, with a design wind load of 45 m/s gust speed. The trackers have a stow position for high wind events.
4.2 BESS (Battery Energy Storage System)

The BESS is rated 20 MW / 40 MWh, comprising 16 containerised units, each with a 1.25 MVA power conversion system. The battery chemistry is lithium iron phosphate (LFP), with a design round-trip efficiency of 90% at 25°C cell temperature. The BESS is connected to the 33 kV auxiliary busbar via a dedicated transformer. The system is configured for frequency regulation, spinning reserve, and peak shaving.

4.3 Auxiliary Power Supply

The station auxiliary power is supplied from two 33 kV station transformers, each rated 15 MVA, with a design load of 12 MVA under normal operating conditions. The auxiliary system is arranged as two independent busbars, each with a standby generator connection. The standby generators are rated 1.5 MVA each, diesel fuelled, with an 8-hour fuel supply at full load.

5. HYDRAULIC SYSTEM

5.1 Headwater and Tailwater Conditions

The plant operates within a headwater elevation range of 114.0 m to 119.0 m, with a normal operating level of 117.0 m. The minimum operating head for turbine operation is 32.5 m, and the maximum design head is 39.0 m. The tailwater elevation varies between 105.0 m and 118.0 m, depending on river discharge and downstream reservoir conditions.

5.2 Hydraulic Head Ranges

The net head for turbine operation is defined as the difference between headwater and tailwater elevations, less the hydraulic losses in the penstock and turbine intake. The design net head is 36.5 m, with a range of 32.5 m to 39.0 m for normal operation. The turbines are designed to operate efficiently within this range, with a minimum net head of 30.0 m for partial load operation.

5.3 Penstock and Intake Design

Each turbine is supplied by an individual penstock, with a design flow of 200 m³/s at the rated net head. The penstock diameter is 5.5 m, with a design pressure of 150 m head. The intake structure includes a trash rack with a bar spacing of 100 mm, and a bulkhead gate for maintenance isolation. The intake is designed for a maximum velocity of 1.5 m/s at full flow.

6. TURBINE GOVERNOR SPECIFICATIONS

6.1 Governor Type and Control

Each turbine is equipped with a digital electro-hydraulic governor, providing speed and load control. The governor is designed for isolated operation with a speed regulation range of ± 0.5%, and for parallel operation with a droop setting adjustable between 2% and 6%. The governor includes a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller with adjustable gains.

6.2 Governor Performance

The governor response time is less than 2 seconds for a 10% load change. The speed rise under full load rejection is limited to 15% of rated speed. The governor is equipped with a load limiter, a speed limiter, and an emergency shutdown valve. The governor is designed for automatic start-up and shutdown sequences.

7. SOLAR PV ARRAY DETAILS

7.1 Module and Mounting

The PV array comprises 132,000 bifacial monocrystalline modules, each rated 455 Wp. The modules are mounted on single-axis trackers with a tilt angle range of 0° to 60°. The trackers are oriented north-south, with a rotation range of ± 45° from the horizontal. The design wind load is 45 m/s gust speed, with a stow position for high wind events.

7.2 Tilt Angle and Orientation

The optimal tilt angle for the array is 10° for the site latitude of 9.6°N. The trackers are programmed to follow the sun from east to west, with a backtracking algorithm to minimise shading. The design ground coverage ratio is 0.45, with a row spacing of 8 m.

7.3 Inverter Stations

The array is divided into 24 inverter stations, each with a 2.5 MVA central inverter. The DC/AC ratio is 1.15. Each inverter station includes a step-up transformer to 33 kV, a DC combiner box, and a monitoring system. The inverters are designed for a maximum ambient temperature of 45°C, with a derating factor of 0.9 at 40°C.

Maintenance Log – Turbine Unit 3 Overhaul Completion

Log Reference: MOU/KJ/2025/LOG-117

Logged By: A. Bello (Maintenance Supervisor, Shift B)

---

Entry 2025-11-16-01

Subject: Completion of Major Overhaul – Turbine Unit 3

Turbine Unit 3 last_overhaul_date was 2025-11-15. Record status: historical. This entry records the formal closure of the major overhaul work order WO-2025-1147, which commenced on 03 November 2025 and was completed on 15 November 2025. The unit has been returned to service and is currently operating under normal load conditions as of the time of this log entry.

The following is a summary of the work performed during the overhaul period. Full detailed reports, including torque values, clearances, and test certificates, are attached to the work order file in the MOU archive (hard copy and digital).

1. Scope of Work – Summary

The overhaul covered the following major components and systems:

- Turbine runner inspection and repair
- Bearing replacement (upper and lower guide bearings)
- Thrust bearing pad inspection and replacement of two worn pads
- Governor system recalibration and linkage adjustment
- Main shaft alignment verification
- Draft tube inspection and debris removal
- Penstock isolation valve operational test
- Cooling water system flush and filter replacement
- Electrical and control system checks (including excitation system)

2. Detailed Work Performed

2.1 Turbine Runner

The runner was inspected for cavitation damage and cracking. Minor cavitation pitting was found on the trailing edge of three blades. The pitting was ground out and welded using the approved procedure (MOU-WELD-04), followed by grinding and polishing to restore the blade profile. Ultrasonic testing was performed on all welds; results were satisfactory. No cracks were found in the runner hub or blade roots.

2.2 Bearings

- Upper guide bearing: Bearing shells were removed and measured. Wear was within acceptable limits, but the bearing was replaced as part of the scheduled overhaul scope. New shells were installed and clearances set to manufacturer specification (0.25 mm ± 0.02 mm).
- Lower guide bearing: Similar to the upper bearing, the lower guide bearing shells were replaced. Oil thrower rings were inspected and found to be in good condition.
- Thrust bearing: All thrust pads were removed and inspected. Two pads showed signs of scoring and were replaced. The remaining pads were within specification. The thrust bearing was re-leveled and the oil film thickness verified during the test run.

2.3 Governor System

The governor was recalibrated. The speed sensing system was checked and the droop setting was adjusted to 4% as per the current grid code requirement. The actuator linkage was inspected for wear; two pins were replaced. The governor was then tested under no-load and load conditions. Response time was within the acceptable range (less than 2 seconds for a 10% load rejection).

2.4 Shaft Alignment

The main shaft alignment was checked using the dial indicator method. The alignment was found to be within the allowable tolerance of 0.05 mm at the coupling. No adjustment was required.

2.5 Draft Tube

The draft tube was inspected and found to contain a small amount of debris (wood fragments and a piece of rope). The debris was removed. The inspection hatch was resealed with a new gasket.

2.6 Penstock Valve

The penstock isolation valve was cycled open and closed three times. The valve operated smoothly with no abnormal vibrations. The valve seals were inspected and found to be in good condition.

The event log also showed that the inverter had attempted three automatic reconnection sequences between 14:36:52 and 14:37:10, all of which failed due to persistent DC bus overvoltage. The inverter then locked out and required manual intervention.

3.3 Diagnostic Findings

The electrical maintenance team (E. Nwachukwu and T. Musa) arrived on site at 15:05 hours. The following checks were performed:

3.3.1 DC Side

- Visual inspection of the DC combiner box connections found no loose terminations, signs of arcing, or discoloration.
- Voltage was measured at the DC input terminals of the inverter. Open circuit voltage was 1,098 VDC, which is within the expected range for the current irradiance and module temperature (~38°C ambient). This indicates the overvoltage event was not caused by an external array condition.
- Insulation resistance was measured on each of the three DC input strings (String 2A, 2B, 2C) using a 1,000 VDC megger. String 2C measured 0.4 MΩ to ground. Strings 2A and 2B both measured greater than 20 MΩ. The low insulation reading on String 2C was isolated by disconnecting the string at the combiner box and re-testing; the fault persisted on the inverter side of the connection, indicating the issue is internal to the inverter's DC bus circuitry rather than the array cabling.

3.3.2 AC Side

Solar Inverter I-7 failure_date was 2026-02-10. Record status: historical.

- The AC output breaker was inspected. No signs of overheating or mechanical damage were found. The breaker was reclosed after the inverter was isolated, and the grid-side voltage was measured at 33.1 kV at the pad-mounted transformer secondary. This is within normal operating range.
- The AC contactor inside the inverter was visually inspected. No visible damage was found, but the contactor was not operated due to the DC-side fault condition.

3.3.3 Thermal and Power Stage

- The IGBT module heatsink was inspected. The cooling fan was found to be operational, but the heatsink fins were partially blocked by dust and plant debris (dried grass and leaves). This is consistent with the E-402 overtemperature code. The debris was removed and the heatsink was cleaned using compressed air.
- Thermal imaging of the IGBT module was performed. The module showed a hotspot at the B-phase switching element. The temperature differential between the B-phase and the A/C phases was 18°C at idle, which is above the 5°C differential limit specified in the manufacturer's service bulletin (SB-IGBT-2024-01).

3.4 Immediate Actions Taken

- The inverter was placed in a locked-out condition with a physical lock and tag applied to the DC disconnect switch. The lock tag number is LOTO-2026-0214.
- The AC breaker was left open and tagged in the open position.

Maintenance Operations Unit (MOU) pending_work_orders_count is 23. Record status: current.

**3.3 Fault Description**

The inverter tripped on error code E-402 (IGBT overtemperature). Initial alarm was received at the central SCADA workstation at 14:05 hours. On dispatch to the inverter pad, the following conditions were noted:

- The DC disconnect switch was found in the closed position, but the inverter was in a fault state.
- The inverter display indicated a simultaneous insulation fault on DC string 2C.
- The cooling fan was running at high speed but appeared to be labouring.

**3.3.1 Electrical Checks**

- Insulation resistance test on DC string 2C was performed using a 1000 V megger. The reading was 0.8 MΩ, which is below the minimum threshold of 1.0 MΩ specified in the plant's commissioning manual. This indicates a degradation of cable insulation, likely due to moisture ingress at the combiner box gland.
- The AC output breaker was inspected. No signs of overheating or mechanical damage were found. The breaker was reclosed after the inverter was isolated, and the grid-side voltage was measured at 33.1 kV at the pad-mounted transformer secondary. This is within normal operating range.
- The AC contactor inside the inverter was visually inspected. No visible damage was found, but the contactor was not operated due to the DC-side fault condition.

**3.3.2 Thermal and Power Stage**

- The IGBT module heatsink was inspected. The cooling fan was found to be operational, but the heatsink fins were partially blocked by dust and plant debris (dried grass and leaves). This is consistent with the E-402 overtemperature code. The debris was removed and the heatsink was cleaned using compressed air.
- Thermal imaging of the IGBT module was performed. The module showed a hotspot at the B-phase switching element. The temperature differential between the B-phase and the A/C phases was 18°C at idle, which is above the 5°C differential limit specified in the manufacturer's service bulletin (SB-IGBT-2024-01).

**3.1 Background and Failure Impact**

Solar Array Alpha comprises 14 string inverters (I-1 through I-14) feeding the 33 kV collection network. On 19 January, inverter I-7 tripped on DC over-voltage and failed to restart. Preliminary diagnostics indicated a failed IGBT module and damage to the DC bus capacitor bank. The vendor’s remote review on 21 January confirmed the unit cannot be repaired on site; a factory replacement is required.

The array’s total peak output is 28.4 MW. Inverter I-7 is one of the two largest units in the array (rated 2.1 MW AC). Its loss reduces the array’s capacity by roughly 7.4% during peak sun hours. Since the failure, the plant has been dispatching the remaining inverters at higher loading, but the DC combiner boxes feeding I-7 are isolated, so no energy is being captured from the affected strings. This is a direct revenue loss, estimated at ₦4.8M per month based on the current PPA tariff and average irradiation for February.

**Safety considerations:** The inverter enclosure contains stored DC voltage even when the AC breaker is open. Any work on the unit requires full DC isolation, use of insulated tools, and a second person present. - **Safety risk:** The failed unit has an active DC bus and exposed capacitor bank. Leaving it in a partially dismantled state increases the risk of arc flash or contact injury to personnel. The area has been barricaded, but a permanent fix is required.
- **Vendor lead time:** The replacement unit is available from the manufacturer’s Lagos warehouse. If ordered this week, delivery is expected within 10 working days. Delaying the order to March would push installation to late March or early April, extending the outage to over two months.

The only other candidate for priority 1 was the turbine hall lighting upgrade (WO-2026-0179), but that is a comfort and safety improvement, not a production-critical failure. The hydraulic pump (WO-2026-0147) is non-critical for normal operation and is already scheduled.

Kainji Hydroelectric and Solar Hybrid Plant – Engineering Specification

Document No: KHP-ENG-SPEC-014 Rev. 4.2
Effective Date: 2026-03-18
Issuing Authority: Plant Engineering Department, Kainji HEP
Status: Current Controlled Document
Supersedes: Rev. 4.1 (dated 2024-11-30, now archived)

1. GENERAL PLANT CAPABILITY

The Kainji Hydroelectric and Solar Hybrid Plant has_capacity_mw is 760 MW. Record status: current. This figure represents the net dependable capacity at the generator terminals under the current operating configuration, including the integrated solar field output during daylight hours. This value is the basis for all system planning, load dispatch agreements, and transmission interface studies. No derating is applied for ambient temperature or reservoir elevation within the normal operating band.

The plant comprises twelve main generating units, a 60 MWp solar PV array on the east embankment, and a 40 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) for grid stabilisation. The solar and BESS components are synchronised through the existing 330 kV switchyard.

2. HYDRAULIC AND CIVIL WORKS

2.1 Dam Structure and Reservoir
The main dam is a zoned earth-fill embankment with a crest length of 8,040 m and a maximum height of 64 m above the lowest foundation level. Structural design safety factor for static loading: 2.0. Dynamic (seismic) safety factor: 1.5, based on a design ground acceleration of 0.08g. The spillway comprises six radial gates, each 12.5 m wide, with a combined discharge capacity of 20,000 m³/s at maximum flood level.

Reservoir top water level (normal): 141.5 m above datum.
Minimum operating level for power generation: 132.0 m above datum.
Usable storage: 11.5 km³.

2.2 Intake and Penstock
Each of the twelve intakes is fitted with a coarse trash rack (bar spacing 120 mm) and a fixed-wheel gate. The penstocks are steel-lined concrete conduits, diameter 6.8 m, with a design head of 38 m at rated flow. Hydraulic design margin on penstock pressure: 15% above maximum static head.

2.3 Tailrace
The tailrace channel is designed for a maximum discharge of 2,800 m³/s without exceeding a tailwater elevation of 118.0 m.

3. ELECTROMECHANICAL EQUIPMENT

3.1 Turbines
Twelve vertical-shaft Francis turbines, each rated at 68 MW at a net head of 36.5 m. Turbine design speed: 100 rpm. Runner diameter: 4.2 m. Each turbine is fitted with a digital electro-hydraulic governor, speed regulation range ± 0.5% under isolated operation.

3.2 Generators
Each turbine is coupled to a 75 MVA synchronous generator, 12 kV, 50 Hz, 0.9 power factor lagging. Generator cooling is closed-circuit air-water, with a design cooling water flow of 1,200 m³/h per unit. Stator winding insulation class F, temperature rise limit 105 K. Excitation is via static thyristor systems with automatic voltage regulation.

3.3 Transformers
Twelve generator step-up transformers, each rated 80 MVA, 12/330 kV, ONAN/ONAF cooling. Impedance: 12.5% at rated MVA. The transformers are located in a dedicated bay adjacent to the powerhouse. Design ambient temperature for loading calculations: 40°C, with a maximum winding hot-spot temperature of 120°C under continuous rated load.

3.4 Switchyard (330 kV)
The 330 kV switchyard is a double-bus, single-breaker arrangement with a total of 14 bays. Circuit breakers are SF6 type, rated 63 kA symmetrical interrupting capacity. Current transformers: 1,200:5 A, class 5P30. The switchyard is designed for a maximum continuous current of 3,150 A per busbar. Busbar design margins are per IEC 62271-1, with a short-time withstand current of 63 kA for 3 seconds.

4. SOLAR PV AND BESS AUXILIARY SYSTEMS

4.1 Solar PV Array
The 60 MWp PV array comprises 132,000 bifacial monocrystalline modules, each rated 455 Wp. The array is divided into 24 inverters stations, each with a 2.5 MVA central inverter. The DC/AC ratio is 1.15. The array is mounted on single-axis trackers, with a design wind load of 45 m/s gust speed. The trackers have a stow position for high wind events.

documents.content:
4.2 BESS (Battery Energy Storage System)

The BESS is rated 20 MW / 40 MWh, comprising 16 containerised units, each with a 1.25 MVA power conversion system. The battery chemistry is lithium iron phosphate (LFP), with a design round-trip efficiency of 90% at 25°C cell temperature. The BESS is connected to the 33 kV auxiliary busbar via a dedicated transformer. The system is configured for frequency regulation, spinning reserve, and peak shaving.

4.3 Auxiliary Power Supply

The station auxiliary power is supplied from two 33 kV station transformers, each rated 15 MVA, with a design load of 12 MVA under normal operating conditions. The auxiliary system is arranged as two independent busbars, each with a standby generator connection. The standby generators are rated 1.5 MVA each, diesel fuelled, with an 8-hour fuel supply at full load.

5. HYDRAULIC SYSTEM

5.1 Headwater and Tailwater Conditions

The plant operates within a headwater elevation range of 114.0 m to 119.0 m, with a normal operating level of 117.0 m. The minimum operating head for turbine operation is 32.5 m, and the maximum design head is 39.0 m. The tailwater elevation varies between 105.0 m and 118.0 m, depending on river discharge and downstream reservoir conditions.

5.2 Hydraulic Head Ranges

The net head for turbine operation is defined as the difference between headwater and tailwater elevations, less the hydraulic losses in the penstock and turbine intake. The design net head is 36.5 m, with a range of 32.5 m to 39.0 m for normal operation. The turbines are designed to operate efficiently within this range, with a minimum net head of 30.0 m for partial load operation.

5.3 Penstock and Intake Design

Each turbine is supplied by an individual penstock, with a design flow of 200 m³/s at the rated net head. The penstock diameter is 5.5 m, with a design pressure of 150 m head. The intake structure includes a trash rack with a bar spacing of 100 mm, and a bulkhead gate for maintenance isolation. The intake is designed for a maximum velocity of 1.5 m/s at full flow.

6. TURBINE GOVERNOR SPECIFICATIONS

6.1 Governor Type and Control

Each turbine is equipped with a digital electro-hydraulic governor, providing speed and load control. The governor is designed for isolated operation with a speed regulation range of ± 0.5%, and for parallel operation with a droop setting adjustable between 2% and 6%. The governor includes a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller with adjustable gains.

6.2 Governor Performance

The governor response time is less than 2 seconds for a 10% load change. The speed rise under full load rejection is limited to 15% of rated speed. The governor is equipped with a load limiter, a speed limiter, and an emergency shutdown valve. The governor is designed for automatic start-up and shutdown sequences.

7. SOLAR PV ARRAY DETAILS

7.1 Module and Mounting

The PV array comprises 132,000 bifacial monocrystalline modules, each rated 455 Wp. The modules are mounted on single-axis trackers with a tilt angle range of 0° to 60°. The trackers are oriented north-south, with a rotation range of ± 45° from the horizontal. The design wind load is 45 m/s gust speed, with a stow position for high wind events.

7.2 Tilt Angle and Orientation

The optimal tilt angle for the array is 10° for the site latitude of 9.6°N. The trackers are programmed to follow the sun from east to west, with a backtracking algorithm to minimise shading. The design ground coverage ratio is 0.45, with a row spacing of 8 m.

7.3 Inverter Stations

The array is divided into 24 inverter stations, each with a 2.5 MVA central inverter. The DC/AC ratio is 1.15. Each inverter station includes a step-up transformer to 33 kV, a DC combiner box, and a monitoring system. The inverters are designed for a maximum ambient temperature of 45°C, with a derating factor of 0.9 at 40°C.

Entry 2025-11-16-01

Subject: Completion of Major Overhaul – Turbine Unit 3

Turbine Unit 3 last_overhaul_date was 2025-11-15. Record status: historical. This entry records the formal closure of the major overhaul work order WO-2025-1147, which commenced on 03 November 2025 and was completed on 15 November 2025. The unit has been returned to service and is currently operating under normal load conditions as of the time of this log entry.

The following is a summary of the work performed during the overhaul period. Full detailed reports, including torque values, clearances, and test certificates, are attached to the work order file in the MOU archive (hard copy and digital).

1. Scope of Work – Summary

The overhaul covered the following major components and systems:

- Turbine runner inspection and repair
- Bearing replacement (upper and lower guide bearings)
- Thrust bearing pad inspection and replacement of two worn pads
- Governor system recalibration and linkage adjustment
- Main shaft alignment verification
- Draft tube inspection and debris removal
- Penstock isolation valve operational test
- Cooling water system flush and filter replacement
- Electrical and control system checks (including excitation system)

2. Detailed Work Performed

2.1 Turbine Runner

The runner was inspected for cavitation damage and cracking. Minor cavitation pitting was found on the trailing edge of three blades. The pitting was ground out and welded using the approved procedure (MOU-WELD-04), followed by grinding and polishing to restore the blade profile. Ultrasonic testing was performed on all welds; results were satisfactory. No cracks were found in the runner hub or blade roots.

2.2 Bearings

- Upper guide bearing: Bearing shells were removed and measured. Wear was within acceptable limits, but the bearing was replaced as part of the scheduled overhaul scope. New shells were installed and clearances set to manufacturer specification (0.25 mm ± 0.02 mm).
- Lower guide bearing: Similar to the upper bearing, the lower guide bearing shells were replaced. Oil thrower rings were inspected and found to be in good condition.
- Thrust bearing: All thrust pads were removed and inspected. Two pads showed signs of scoring and were replaced. The remaining pads were within specification. The thrust bearing was re-leveled and the oil film thickness verified during the test run.

2.3 Governor System

The governor was recalibrated. The speed sensing system was checked and the droop setting was adjusted to 4% as per the current grid code requirement. The actuator linkage was inspected for wear; two pins were replaced. The governor was then tested under no-load and load conditions. Response time was within the acceptable range (less than 2 seconds for a 10% load rejection).

2.4 Shaft Alignment

The main shaft alignment was checked using the dial indicator method. The alignment was found to be within the allowable tolerance of 0.05 mm at the coupling. No adjustment was required.

2.5 Draft Tube

The draft tube was inspected and found to contain a small amount of debris (wood fragments and a piece of rope). The debris was removed. The inspection hatch was resealed with a new gasket.

2.6 Penstock Valve

The penstock isolation valve was cycled open and closed three times. The valve operated smoothly with no abnormal vibrations. The valve seals were inspected and found to be in good condition.

The MOU staffing records show that the Maintenance Operations Unit (MOU) technicians_available_2026_q1 is 18. Record status: current. Estimates are based on the current Maintenance and Operations Understanding (MOU) with the asset owners, except where noted as revised or provisional. All hours are technician-hours, not calendar hours.

3.1 Hydraulic Pump HP-2 (Pump 2)

Hydraulic Pump HP-2 maintenance_hours_required is 12 hours. Record status: current. This estimate is current and was confirmed in the MOU review meeting on 12 December 2025; it has not been revised since the pump’s last overhaul in September 2025.

The 12-hour figure covers the following tasks:

- Full inspection of the pump casing and impeller wear rings
- Replacement of the two shaft seals (parts already in stores, P/N HP2-SEAL-01 and HP2-SEAL-02)
- Flushing of the hydraulic oil circuit and replacement of the oil filter
- Functional test under load, including vibration and temperature logging

The job requires two qualified mechanical technicians working together for safety reasons, as the pump is located in a confined pit below the turbine hall floor. With two technicians, the job takes approximately 6 calendar hours on site, plus 1 hour for preparation and 1 hour for documentation and cleanup. This is why the estimate is 12 technician-hours rather than 6.

Skills required: mechanical (rotating equipment) – Senior Technician preferred for the seal replacement; a Junior Technician can assist under supervision. The electrical team is not required for this job, as the pump motor is not being opened. The solar team is not involved.

Scheduling constraints:

- The pump pit must be isolated and locked out before work begins. This requires coordination with the electrical team for the motor breaker lockout/tagout, which takes 30 minutes and is counted within the 12 hours.
- The job should be done on a weekday, preferably Tuesday to Thursday, because the confined space entry permit requires the safety officer to be on site. The safety officer is not available on Mondays (weekly planning meeting) or Fridays (site walkdown with the client).
- The pump is not critical for normal plant operation, but it is used during the monthly hydraulic system test on the first Monday of each month. The maintenance window must therefore avoid the first Monday of any month in Q1. January’s first Monday is the 5th, February’s is the 2nd, and March’s is the 2nd. All other days in the quarter are acceptable.
- The work order (WO-2026-0147) has been raised and is currently in “Planned” status. It has not yet been assigned a start date, pending the final allocation in Section 5 of this report.

**3. SOLAR ARRAY ALPHA – INVERTER REPLACEMENT (WO-2026-0188)**

**3.1 Background and Failure Impact**

Solar Array Alpha comprises 14 string inverters (I-1 through I-14) feeding the 33 kV collection network. On 19 January, inverter I-7 tripped on DC over-voltage and failed to restart. Preliminary diagnostics indicated a failed IGBT module and damage to the DC bus capacitor bank. The vendor’s remote review on 21 January confirmed the unit cannot be repaired on site; a factory replacement is required.

The array’s total peak output is 28.4 MW. Inverter I-7 is one of the two largest units in the array (rated 2.1 MW AC). Its loss reduces the array’s capacity by roughly 7.4% during peak sun hours. Since the failure, the plant has been dispatching the remaining inverters at higher loading, but the DC combiner boxes feeding I-7 are isolated, so no energy is being captured from the affected strings. This is a direct revenue loss, estimated at ₦4.8M per month based on the current PPA tariff and average irradiation for February.

**Safety considerations:** The inverter enclosure contains stored DC voltage even when the AC breaker is open. Any work on the unit requires full DC isolation, use of insulated tools, and a second person present. The replacement procedure includes discharging the DC bus capacitors and verifying zero voltage before disconnecting the old unit. The vendor’s installation team is certified for this work; our in-house electricians will provide lockout/tagout and site supervision only.

**3.2 Priority Ranking**

Solar Array Alpha inverter_replacement_priority is Solar Inverter I-7. Record status: current. This ranking was confirmed by the Maintenance Operations Unit on 2 February and is current as of this report. The ranking considers:

- **Production impact:** I-7 is the largest failed inverter in the array. No other inverter at Alpha is currently off-line.
- **Revenue loss:** The longer I-7 remains out of service, the greater the lost generation. The estimated monthly loss exceeds the cost of the replacement unit.
- **Safety risk:** The failed unit has an active DC bus and exposed capacitor bank. Leaving it in a partially dismantled state increases the risk of arc flash or contact injury to personnel. The area has been barricaded, but a permanent fix is required.
- **Vendor lead time:** The replacement unit is available from the manufacturer’s Lagos warehouse. If ordered this week, delivery is expected within 10 working days. Delaying the order to March would push installation to late March or early April, extending the outage to over two months.

The only other candidate for priority 1 was the turbine hall lighting upgrade (WO-2026-0179), but that is a comfort and safety improvement, not a production-critical failure. The hydraulic pump (WO-2026-0147) is non-critical for normal operation and is already scheduled.

**3.3 Budget and Procurement**

The committee approved ₦4.2M for this job, broken down as follows:

- Replacement inverter unit (refurbished, with 12-month warranty): ₦3,150,000
- Shipping and customs clearance (Lagos to site): ₦210,000
- Vendor installation team (2 technicians, 2 days, including travel and accommodation): ₦640,000
- Consumables (DC cable lugs, torque sealant, replacement fuses): ₦120,000
- Contingency (10%): ₦80,000

The purchase order (PO-2026-0331) was raised on 3 February and is awaiting the supplier’s invoice. The vendor has confirmed the unit is held for us until 12 February. If the PO is not released by then, the unit will be released to another customer and the lead time extends to 6 weeks.
